name: DLQ Judge
statusNote: Hackathon prototype. The repository's deployment report records a deploy to us-east-1 on 18 Oct 2026; current availability is not confirmed.
summary: A confidence-gated agent that triages Amazon SQS dead-letter queues. For each failed message it redrives, quarantines, discards or escalates, and asks Amazon Bedrock for a second opinion only when it is unsure.

caseStudy.problem: Failed messages pile up in SQS dead-letter queues. Manual triage does not scale, and blindly redriving or deleting is unsafe. Operators need an agent that acts only when the evidence is strong and escalates when it is not.
approach: Each message gets one of five actions: redrive now, redrive later, quarantine the payload in S3, discard a confirmed duplicate, or escalate to a human.
Strands Decider 2B scores the options. At 0.85 or above the agent acts; between 0.60 and 0.85 it asks Amazon Bedrock and acts only if Bedrock agrees; below 0.60 it escalates.
The decision logic ships as a reusable module, patterns/confidence-gated-action, with typed options, thresholds, guards and a pluggable Bedrock interface.

architecture.caption: Confidence-gated triage. Hover or focus a component to see its role.

nodes.label: SQS DLQ
nodes.note: Dead-letter queues for the orders, payments and shipping queues hold failed messages.

nodes.label: DLQ Judge agent
nodes.note: Reads messages, masks PII, and asks the decider for the safest next action.

nodes.label: Decider 2B
nodes.note: Strands Decider 2B returns a probability per action. Its confidence picks the path.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock
nodes.note: Second opinion, used only in the 0.60 to 0.85 band so cost and latency stay low.

nodes.label: Actions
nodes.note: Applied only with --apply. The default run is a dry run.

nodes.label: Escalate / report
nodes.note: Low confidence or disagreement leaves the message for a human.

nodes.label: SQS redrive
nodes.note: Retry immediately or after a delay to the source queue.

nodes.label: S3 quarantine
nodes.note: Poison payloads are parked in S3 for engineering.

nodes.label: Delete duplicate
nodes.note: Guarded: needs at least 0.90 confidence and an idempotency key.

nodes.label: Audit report
nodes.note: Every run writes a per-run audit log.

decisions: Bedrock is called only in the uncertain band, so confident decisions cost nothing extra and stay fast.
Discarding is treated as the riskiest action and needs both 0.90 confidence and an idempotency key.
A CPU instance (t3.xlarge) was chosen because the account's GPU instance quota was zero; this is recorded in the deployment report.
security: Dry run by default; mutating actions require an explicit --apply flag.
PII is masked before anything reaches the decider or the logs.
IAM is scoped to the dlqj-* queues, the quarantine bucket and Bedrock invoke.
The EC2 security group accepts traffic only from the CloudFront prefix list. There is no SSH; administration goes through Systems Manager.
deployment: One CloudFormation stack creates the SQS queues and DLQs, S3 buckets, Cognito user pool, IAM roles, the EC2 instance and a CloudFront distribution.
The app is packaged to S3 and installed as a systemd service through SSM Run Command.
AWS Budgets definitions live in the repository's infra folder.

results.text: On a 300-message benchmark, every approach had a 0% unsafe-action rate. Accuracy was 100% for the rules baseline and 6.7% for both Bedrock-only and DLQ Judge, so the agent does not yet beat simple rules on this dataset.
Estimated running cost about $0.17 per hour while the instance is on (t3.xlarge plus storage).

limitations: Benchmark accuracy shows the decider needs more work before it can replace rules.
Demo video and live app links in the README are still placeholders.

name: IncidentLens
statusNote: Sample project. Not deployed anywhere; no production traffic claims (per its README).
summary: Lightweight incident detection for SRE-style workflows. It ingests structured JSON logs, detects repeated errors and error-rate spikes against a baseline, and dedupes them into incidents you can acknowledge and resolve.

caseStudy.problem: Raw logs bury the signal. On-call engineers need repeated errors and abnormal error rates grouped into a small number of incidents with a clear lifecycle, not thousands of lines.
approach: Logs arrive through a REST API or a CLI that reads JSONL.
A pure detection engine fingerprints messages, flags repeats inside a sliding window, and compares recent counts against a historical baseline.
Ongoing issues are deduped into incidents that move through open, acknowledged and resolved.

architecture.caption: Thin adapters around a pure detection core.

nodes.label: CLI (JSONL)
nodes.note: Exit code 1 when incidents are created or updated, 0 when none, 2 on errors, so it can gate a pipeline.

nodes.label: REST API
nodes.note: POST /logs, GET and PATCH /incidents, GET /health. OpenAPI docs at /docs.

nodes.label: IncidentService
nodes.note: Owns ingest, detect, and create-or-bump incident.

nodes.label: DetectionEngine
nodes.note: No I/O. Fingerprints, repeat thresholds and baseline comparison, all unit-testable.

nodes.label: IncidentRepository
nodes.note: Parameterised queries only.

nodes.label: SQLite (WAL)
nodes.note: Single-process store on a Docker volume.

decisions: Detection has no I/O, so thresholds and fingerprinting are tested without a database.
All tuning lives in environment variables with an INCIDENTLENS_ prefix: repeat threshold, window, baseline multiplier and a cold-start guard.
The CLI's exit codes make it usable as a CI or cron gate.
security: Pydantic validation with size limits on messages and batches.
Validation errors return structured field errors instead of echoing request bodies.
Parameterised SQL queries; the container runs as a non-root user.
No secrets in the repository; configuration comes from the environment.
deployment: Runs locally with make run, or with docker compose up --build.
Tests cover the API, CLI, detection engine, fingerprinting and service layers.
limitations: Single-process SQLite, not a multi-writer store.
The baseline is a simple per-fingerprint window average, not seasonal.
The API has no authentication; it is a local sample.

name: ErrorSaathi
statusNote: Built in a few hours at a hackathon. Some features are early prototypes (per its README).
summary: A CI doctor for open-source contributors. Give it a GitHub PR, a log or a screenshot and it explains what failed, why, and how to fix it in English or Roman Urdu, labelling every command SAFE, CAUTION or DESTRUCTIVE.

caseStudy.problem: First-time contributors see a red CI check, face a long and cryptic log, and give up. Documentation is mostly in English, and maintainers explain the same failures again and again.
approach: Fetch the PR, failed workflow jobs, job logs and diff from the GitHub REST API, or accept a pasted log, file or screenshot.
Clean the log, keep the lines around errors, and redact secrets before any model call.

A zero-cost regex router sends simple failures to a single fast call and complex ones through Triage, Investigator, Fixer and Safety Reviewer agents. A Blame agent maps errors to the changed file and line.

architecture.caption: Redaction happens before inference; posting needs explicit confirmation.

nodes.label: PR / log / screenshot
nodes.note: GitHub PR URL, pasted log, .log or .txt upload, or an error screenshot.

nodes.label: GitHub API
nodes.note: PR details, workflow runs, failed jobs, job logs and the diff.

nodes.label: Preprocess
nodes.note: Strip ANSI codes, collapse repeats, keep error windows, truncate long logs.

nodes.label: Redact secrets
nodes.note: Masks AWS keys, GitHub and GitLab tokens, JWTs, passwords, private keys, connection strings and emails.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.note: Regex detection of technology and signals. No API call.

nodes.label: Fast mode
nodes.note: One Gemma call for simple failures.

nodes.label: Multi-agent path
nodes.note: Triage, Investigator, Fixer, then Safety Reviewer.

nodes.label: Blame agent
nodes.note: Correlates errors with the PR diff to suggest the file and line.

nodes.label: Diagnosis
nodes.note: English or Roman Urdu, with SAFE / CAUTION / DESTRUCTIVE labels.

nodes.label: Confirm → PR comment
nodes.note: Posted only after the user previews and confirms.

decisions: A free regex router decides fast versus deep analysis before spending any model calls.
Two Gemma 4 models with automatic fallback, retries with backoff on 429 and 503, and a cache keyed on a hash of the redacted log.
Log windowing and truncation cut the tokens sent to the model.
security: Advise-only: the app never executes generated commands or changes infrastructure.
Destructive patterns such as rm -rf, kubectl delete and terraform destroy are flagged.
Keys live in git-ignored files; GitHub push protection and secret scanning are enabled on the repository (per README).
deployment: Runs with Streamlit locally; optional deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud with secrets in its settings.
A GitHub Actions workflow lives in .github/workflows/ci.yml.
limitations: AI output can be wrong and must be reviewed.
The Blame agent may not always find the exact file and line.
Very large logs are truncated, and free-tier model quotas limit throughput.

name: AWS 3-Tier Architecture
statusNote: Learning project built step by step in the AWS console. No Terraform (per its README).
summary: A secure three-tier network on AWS: an Application Load Balancer for users, OpenVPN as the only admin path to SSH, and a Squid proxy as the controlled way out for private servers.

caseStudy.problem: Application servers should not be reachable from the internet, admins still need SSH, and private servers still need packages. Each path needs its own, narrow door.
approach: One VPC with four subnets, an internet gateway, and separate public and private route tables in ap-south-1.
Users reach the frontend and backend only through the ALB, with path routing for /api/*.
Admins connect through OpenVPN, locked to their own IP, before SSH. Private hosts reach the internet only through Squid.

architecture.caption: Three doors: ALB for users, OpenVPN for admins, Squid for egress.

nodes.label: Users
nodes.note: Browser traffic only.

nodes.label: Admin (MyIP)
nodes.note: The VPN security group allows only the admin's public IP.

nodes.label: ALB :80
nodes.note: APP security group. Target groups for frontend and /api/* backend.

nodes.label: OpenVPN :1194
nodes.note: Public host with an Elastic IP; the only way to reach SSH.

nodes.label: Frontend :80
nodes.note: Private subnet, no public IP. Web security group.

nodes.label: Backend :8000
nodes.note: Private subnet, no public IP. /api/health returns ok.

nodes.label: SSH :22
nodes.note: Connect security group allows SSH only from the VPN.

nodes.label: Squid :8888
nodes.note: Proxy security group. Private hosts send outbound traffic here.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.note: Package repositories, reached only through the proxy.

decisions: One security group per role (APP, Web, Backend, Proxy, Remote, VPN, Connect) keeps every rule narrow and readable.
No public IPs on application servers.
A documented cleanup order (ALB, target groups, instances, EIP, security groups, subnets, VPC) because the ALB is billed.
security: SSH is reachable only through the VPN, and the VPN only from the admin's IP.
Private servers have controlled egress through a proxy instead of a NAT to everything.
deployment: Built from a master checklist and a step-by-step DEPLOY.md, with boot scripts in userdata/.
Tested by checking the ALB DNS, /api/health, healthy target groups, VPN-to-SSH and the proxy path.
limitations: Manual console build; no infrastructure as code yet.

name: InfraPilot AI
statusNote: Runs locally with clearly labelled demo data; live Bedrock mode is optional. Hosted status not confirmed.
summary: AWS architecture design and review. Describe requirements or upload a diagram, get security, cost, reliability and scalability gaps with evidence, an optimised design, and Draw.io, PNG and Excel exports.

caseStudy.problem: Architecture reviews are slow and inconsistent. Teams need a repeatable way to check a design for security, cost, reliability and scalability gaps before building it.
approach: Capture business requirements, then generate an architecture with Amazon Bedrock or upload an existing Draw.io file.
A deterministic rules engine returns Pass, Fail, Warning, Unknown or Not Applicable, kept separate from AI suggestions.
Propose an optimised design and compare it with the original.

architecture.caption: Serverless: static SPA plus a Lambda API.

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.note: Vite single-page app.

nodes.label: CloudFront + S3
nodes.note: Hosts the static frontend.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.note: HTTP API in front of the backend.

nodes.label: Lambda (FastAPI)
nodes.note: FastAPI wrapped with Mangum.

nodes.label: Bedrock (optional)
nodes.note: Generation and gap suggestions. DEMO_MODE avoids Bedrock spend.

nodes.label: DynamoDB
nodes.note: Project history.

nodes.label: S3 artifacts
nodes.note: Exports and uploads.

nodes.label: CloudWatch Logs
nodes.note: Function logs.

decisions: Rules first, AI second: the deterministic engine gives evidence, the model adds suggestions.
Scope boundary: the product designs and reviews architectures only and never deploys customer infrastructure.
Demo mode with labelled sample data keeps development free of model spend.
security: The deploy workflow assumes an AWS role through GitHub OIDC; no long-lived AWS keys are stored in the repository.
Bedrock access is optional and off in demo mode.
deployment: CI runs Ruff, pytest, a Lambda package smoke build and the frontend build on every change.
A separate deploy workflow ships the backend and frontend to AWS.
limitations: PNG export is a placeholder diagram (per README).
